references.text: The psalmist cries out to God for mercy with the words "Be merciful to me" (ἐλέησόν με), the same plea for compassion that the lepers direct to Jesus. [ref:Ps 57:2|Psalms 57:2]
Simon Peter addresses Jesus as "ἐπιστάτα" (Master), the same form of address used by the lepers in their prayer to Jesus. [ref:Lk 5:5|Luke 5:5]
The disciples use the title "ἐπιστάτα" (Master) when they cry out to Jesus for help in the storm, paralleling the desperate cries of the lepers. [ref:Lk 8:24|Luke 8:24]
The blind man at Jericho cries out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" (ἐλέησόν με) – the same type of plea for compassion that the lepers make. [ref:Lk 18:38-39|Luke 18:38-39]
Two blind men follow Jesus and cry out, "Have mercy on us" (ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς), using exactly the same expression as the lepers. [ref:Mt 9:27|Matthew 9:27]
Two blind men cry out to Jesus, "Lord, have mercy on us" (ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς), with the same wording found in the lepers' prayer. [ref:Mt 20:30-31|Matthew 20:30-31]
The Canaanite woman cries out, "Lord, have mercy on me" (ἐλέησόν με), an expression of faith and desperate prayer that resembles the lepers' cry. [ref:Mt 15:22|Matthew 15:22]
A father asks Jesus to "have mercy on my son" (ἐλέησόν μου τὸν υἱόν), the same plea for compassion directed to Jesus. [ref:Mt 17:15|Matthew 17:15]
The ten lepers who met Jesus and stood at a distance, providing the context for their cry for mercy. [ref:Lk 17:12|Luke 17:12]
The law required that lepers keep apart and cry out "Unclean, unclean!" – the background explaining why the lepers stood at a distance and cried out to Jesus. [ref:Lev 13:45-46|Leviticus 13:45-46]
